turns.speaker: A
turns.text: When you start building hardware projects, debugging feels very different from software. Why is that?

turns.speaker: B
turns.text: In software, the problem is almost always in your code. In hardware, it could be the code, the wiring, the power supply, the sensor, or even electrical noise in the room.

turns.speaker: B
turns.text: I start by checking the physical things. Hardware troubleshooting often begins with loose wires, wrong pins or a bad connection on the breadboard. It's surprising how often that's the problem.

turns.speaker: B
turns.text: Power is the next suspect. Many strange bugs happen because the board doesn't get enough stable power. A cheap USB cable or weak battery can cause random resets.

turns.speaker: B
turns.text: That's when unwanted electrical interference changes your readings. Long wires, motors and nearby devices can all cause it. You might see a sensor value jumping around for no reason.

turns.speaker: B
turns.text: The simplest and most useful one is the serial monitor. Your microcontroller prints messages to your computer while it runs, so you can see what it's doing. A cheap multimeter is also great for checking voltages.

turns.speaker: B
turns.text: Change only one thing at a time. If you change the code and the wiring together, you'll never know which one fixed the problem.
